title: All scripture (2 Timothy 3:14–17)
hookLine: scripture is inspired and useful for teaching and correcting (CCC 105)

lines: ONE GREEK WORD IN SECOND TIMOTHY.
cards: Hold your hand in front of your mouth and breathe out slowly. Warm, moving, there and then gone. Today's word is inspiration, the word the Church uses for what it teaches about the Bible.

Behind it stands a single Greek word, near the end of the second letter to Timothy. Paul is reminding his young friend of the scriptures he has known since he was a child, and then he says what they are.

teach.b: From infancy, Paul says, you have known the holy scriptures. For Timothy, that meant the Jewish scriptures, what Christians call the Old Testament; the New was still being written.
Then: "All scripture, inspired of God, is profitable to teach, to reprove, to correct, to instruct in justice, That the man of God may be perfect, furnished to every good work."
Inspired of God is one Greek word: theopneustos. Theos, God. Pneō, to breathe.
God-breathed. It may remind a reader of Genesis, where God breathes into the first man and he becomes a living soul. In that picture, the words on the page carry God's breath.
To teach and to reprove are about what to believe. To correct and to instruct in justice are about how to live. It's a working tool, so the person of God is equipped for every good work.
What do Catholics mean by inspiration? The Catechism says God is the author of Sacred Scripture.

teach.h: GOD AND HUMAN AUTHORS, BOTH TRUE.
teach.b: But the Second Vatican Council adds something important: the human writers were true authors too. God chose them and used them, with their own powers and abilities, their language, their style, their era.
So a reader can hear Paul's temper and Luke's careful research and the psalmist's grief, and the Church still calls the words God's.
The Council says the books teach firmly, faithfully and without error the truth God wanted put into writing for the sake of our salvation.
And it says Scripture must be read in the same Spirit in which it was written. For Catholics, that means reading it within the Church, together with Tradition.
Breathed out once, the Church says, and breathed in every time it's read.

how: Catholics hear Scripture at every Mass and many practice lectio divina, slow prayerful reading; the Church teaches that Scripture is inspired by God and is read within the living Tradition of the Church.

o: God-breathed: Scripture with God as its author
a sudden good idea that comes to a writer
the feeling of being moved by a good sermon

games.q: inside the word — tap the pairs.

s: 'Scripture' in this verse meant the New Testament
for Timothy it meant the Jewish scriptures; the New Testament was still being written.
in this verse, 'inspired of God' is a single Greek word
Catholics believe the human writers were only secretaries taking dictation
Vatican II says they were true authors, using their own powers.

games.q: Paul tells Timothy what scripture is for. which does he name?
o: teaching, reproving, correcting and instructing in justice.
predicting the date of the end.
games.why: "profitable to teach, to reprove, to correct, to instruct in justice, that the man of God may be perfect, furnished to every good work."

practice: Choose any verse you know, or today's, all scripture, inspired of God, and say it slowly in your head three times: notice which word stands out, then stay with that one word as you breathe in and out.
If you pray, answer it with a word of your own; if not, notice what one slow verse does to the next minute.

wordCard.voice: Inspiration. From the Greek theopneustos, God-breathed: Catholics believe Scripture has God as its author, written through true human authors. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: God-breathed, from theos (God) and pneō (to breathe), in 2 Timothy 3:16.

carryVoice: Your line: god-breathed. God's words, written by people with their own voices. See you tomorrow.
